title: The Samoan Women Who Defied a Flu
event_summary: When the 1918 influenza pandemic swept the Pacific, the SS Talune carried it to Western Samoa (then under New Zealand administration), where it killed roughly 22% of the population in weeks. Just 70 miles away, American Samoa's governor, Commander John Martin Poyer, imposed an immediate and total maritime quarantine, refusing all ships entry. Local Samoan women organized village-level enforcement, turning away boats and monitoring shorelines, ensuring not a single influenza death was recorded on the islands.
why_forgotten: Western Samoa's catastrophic losses were an embarrassment to New Zealand's colonial administration, which actively downplayed comparisons. American Samoa's success was credited almost exclusively to Poyer in official records, erasing the Indigenous community's role in enforcement. The Pacific Islands rarely feature in global pandemic histories dominated by European and American narratives.
why_it_matters: American Samoa's zero-death outcome became one of history's most successful quarantine case studies, directly cited by epidemiologists modeling responses to SARS, Ebola, and COVID-19. It demonstrated that swift border closure and community-level cooperation could entirely stop a respiratory pandemic — a lesson many governments failed to apply a century later. The contrast between the two Samoas also became foundational evidence for how colonial negligence amplifies disease mortality.
